utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Judge Fluegge is, for urgent reasons, not able to sit today. Therefore, for a limited time, Judge Moloto and myself, we have considered whether it would be in the interests of justice to continue hearing the case under Rule 15 bis, and we decided it was. Therefore, we'll proceed. There are a few matters which are of some urgency, and therefore I would like to deal with them first before we ask the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. First, on the 20th of November, 2013, the Prosecution announced that it may make further submissions about adducing evidence which had not been adduced in reliance on certain adjudicated facts, which have now been vacated. The Prosecution also announced the tendering of one additional witness. The Chamber requests the Prosecution to file any such motions no later than the 2nd of December, 2013. Then we briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The next item I'd like to deal with briefly is the Prosecution's announcement of tendering proof of death documents. On the 18th of November of this year, the Prosecution announced its intention to tender approximately 1400 documents underlying the expert report, P2797, of Witness Tabeau. The Prosecution argued that (a), even taking Witness Tabeau's evidence at its highest without the actual documents in evidence, the Chamber might have been left curious as to how certain information was gathered and how conclusions were drawn in the report, which analyses these document. And, (b), that all victims deserved to be named as a victim in the final judgement. The Chamber recalls its previous guidance that underlying documents to expert reports should, as a general rule, not be tendered into evidence. More specifically on the 17th of October the Chamber stated the following - and I quote - in its correspondence in relation to Witness Tabeau, the Prosecution states: "Should the Chamber find she is an expert and admit her POD expert report, it's not the Prosecution intention, as a general rule, to tender documents related to victims which are not specifically challenged by the Mladic Defence, absent a specific challenge the Prosecution considers tendering the underlying documents may, in most cases, be unnecessary." And then I continue with the quote from what the Chamber said: "Based on this, the Chamber understands that the Prosecution will proceed in accordance with the Chamber's guidance with respect to Witness Tabeau. With regard to the Prosecution's reference to wanting to tender 2.000 documents with Witness Tabeau, the Chamber then understands that this is only so if the Defence specifically challenges the expert's finding in relation to each victim." And now I'm at the end of the quote of what the Chamber said. The Prosecution has not argued that the Defence challenged specific findings of the expert. Witness Tabeau's report, P2797, is extremely lengthy, at 656 pages, and any open questions as to how she drew certain conclusions could have been asked during her examinations. Furthermore, the Chamber does not consider that every victim of a crime necessarily needs to be mentioned in the final judgement by name, individually by name. Tendering a large number of underlying documents risks duplicating the sources needed to make a factual finding in relation to the death of individuals. The Prosecution has not argued and it does not appear that the underlying documents have any additional value vis-à-vis the expert report. Under these circumstances, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution's anticipated tendering does not assist the Chamber and strongly encourages it to re-evaluate its approach prior to any further submissions on this matter. Then I move to the next item. In a filing of the 20th of November, 2013, the Prosecution indicated that it would re-call Witness Barry Hogan as a result of the Appeals Chamber's decision on adjudicated facts. The Chamber considers this as a request to be permitted to call Hogan for additional evidence. Now, before deciding, could the Defence state its position as to the request of the Prosecution to be permitted to call Mr. Hogan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the request to re-call Mr. Hogan is granted. We will now move on to hear the evidence of the witness. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, as he is brought in, I just wanted to note the last document from yesterday, the minutes from the 11th Session of the Sanski Most Municipality Assembly Executive Council, we've uploaded matching versions under 65 ter 06442A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown. Mr. Brown, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then if we can see in the e-court 06442A. This is record from the 11th Session of executive committee of municipality of Sanski Most. And we need page 5 in B/C/S. And since I haven't seen the English version yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe it will be page 3 in the English, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. [Interpretation] We can see and we will start with Kalacun. You will find his name on the top of the English page. We need page 5 in B/C/S. Page 5 in e-court. I don't know whether we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It -- I think, based on the re-upload, it may be page 4 in e-court and I'd ask -- and I'd suggest the third and fourth speakers from the top are what Mr. Lukic may be looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, we can see that Mr. Kalacun first said as follows: "I would like to ask the IO chairman and to inform us of the general position of the Krajina AR government on the exodus from the Serbian state." Nedeljko Rasula responds and says: "There is no general position, there are no instructions, nobody is forced to go into exile. The basic principle is that citizens should decide where they want to live. If they want to leave, they should be allowed to leave with a certain supervision and protection. Those who wish to remain in the municipality will be allowed to stay, only if they have not participated in any underhand activities. Those who wish to leave will have to cover the costs of their journey, because we have no resources for this. "M. Lukic: According to international law, exodus cannot be prevented anywhere. Those who wish to leave should be helped to do so, and those who wish to stay should be allowed to stay." Mr. Brown, were you aware of this document when you were drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I was. Could I see the date of the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you can see, the minutes were taken on the 14th of August, 1992, during the 11th Session of this body.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to comment on the document, sir, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, I have questions for you that I wish to ask you. First of all, would you agree with me that this document was exactly contrary to your conclusion in paragraph 2.160? I'm referring to your report, sir.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't necessarily think it's contrary to the report at all. I think by this time a large number of non-Serbs had already -- well, (a) there had been attacks on non-Serb areas, a significant number of non-Serbs had left or were in detention centres, and the timing of this document comes around when there was significant international pressure as a result of the media visits by international agencies and pressure by the international community in the negotiations. And the document says what it says, and some of the delegates, as you've read out, indicate what they say. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, according to you, this document is not contrary, does not contradict your own findings.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would have to read the whole document, and as I say, I would argue that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the part of the document that we have just read out. According to you, does this part of the document contradict your own findings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think that the witness has -- what was read to him, he said it would not change and then he said apart from that I would like to look at the whole of the document. So he has answered your question. And it's also fair if the witness wants to see the whole of the document to allow him. Not at this moment. If you would give him a copy then he would see, perhaps, the deals of how people were -- had to be transported on buses and how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For me, it is enough that he says that this part of the document is not in contradiction with his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With his findings. And we will propose this document into evidence. So now we have this A version which has translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, it would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06442A receives number D432, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D432 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will look at another document pertaining to that same area. As a matter of fact, we'll see two documents. First of all, let's look at 1D1456. Did we see the same document yesterday perhaps? No, I'm sorry. We already saw this document. I'm interested in seeing another one, which is 1D1457.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, we can see -- just a moment. It's a document in which Dr. Radovan Karadzic issued an order. The document was issued on the 23rd of July, 1992, before foreign journalists arrived and before all the pressure was put on the government. I apologise. Did you perhaps not hear me? 23rd July 1992 is the date when this document was issued, before foreign journalists arrived, and I'm referring to Gutman and Penny Marshall and others; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Gutman actually arrived on the 16th of July, in and around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did he publish his first texts?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe at the end of that month. So it might have been after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this order, in paragraph 2, President Karadzic orders as follows: "All inhabitants who surrender weapons and agree to live peacefully and in keeping with the law must be enabled to remain in their own homes and enjoy our protection." Does this document contradict your findings, sir?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it does. I think it puts into context -- I mean, at the beginning of the document it's talking about negotiations at the London Conference, and at this time there was already information coming out that -- well, first of all, there was already information coming out in the international community that pressure was coming on the Bosnian Serbs that this was happening. This is it -- and it wasn't just Penny Marshall or Gutman that was creating this issue. And by this time, large numbers of people had already been moved out but there were -- many thousands were already in detention centres. This document doesn't say, We should release all these individuals. It doesn't give any indication as to why is it that the conditions are so bad that these people want to move out? That there's a lot --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would agree -- so you would agree that this document is perfectly in line with your own findings.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is either in line of your findings or not. I don't need any lengthy explanations. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a simple yes or no issue. You know that and it makes no sense to present it as if it were. Please proceed. You have asked a question. The witness has answered. He has explained why he considers the context of this document such that it does not contradict his findings so, therefore, that is an explained no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we will move on to another topic: Preventing looting and prohibiting looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.186 of your report, are your findings which are discussed in paragraphs 2.168 through 2.186. You say that looting was allowed, providing that the looted goods ended up in the coffers of the corps and not in the pockets of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. As regards the previous document that we showed to the witness, which is Dr. Karadzic's order, is being tendered into evidence. The document number is 1D1457.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that document would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D433 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'd like to call up 1D1465. As a matter of fact, this document has been admitted as 1D576 -- or perhaps not in our case. I apologise. 1D1465 is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a very short document, which was issued by the command of the 30th Partizan Battalion on the 3rd of June, 1992, and under 1 it says: "At all costs, prevent looting, arson, and private wars in the zone of responsibility of the division. "Protect refugees and innocent people and treat the surrendering enemy according to the international law on prisoners of war. "Take the most drastic legal and other measures up to and including physical liquidation against those who violate this order." Physical liquidation of one's own troop is a rather extreme measure when it comes to disciplining one's troops. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir. I didn't see any examples in the documents I reviewed that that actually happened. But, no, I do agree with your point that physical liquidation of your own troops is the ultimate sanction, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document is a military secret. It was not intended for the media. It was for internal purposes only; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's within the commander's.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The date when this document was issued is the 3rd of June, 1992. You will agree with me that the document was issued before any international pressure was put to bear?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I do know of some other examples in the collection of similar instructions about -- which I reference and openly reference in the report about behaviour, including references from the Main Staff and -- and references from the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You agree with me, won't you, that no distinction is made here between those who engage in looting for their own personal gain or for the gain of their corps; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't make distinction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D434, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at 65 ter 16585. It is a Prosecutor's document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document was issued by the command of the 5th Corps prior to the corps -- the corps' renaming. The Army of Republika Srpska was established on the 12th of May, and a decision was made -- then taken on its establishment. This document was sent to 33 different addressees which can be seen from the last page. And under 2, it says: "2(a), raise the problem of criminal activity at all military gatherings and meetings at all levels daily, pointing out crime, particularly cases of looting, theft, and looting of private property, rape and ill-treatment of the local population regardless of their ethnic background. Anyone who has committed such crimes should be named, publicly shamed and arrested, unless this has been done already, in front of all the troops." Further on, it says: "Should these persons offer resistance during their arrest or attempt to escape, apply the toughest possible physical methods, including the use of fire-arms." Would you agree with me that this was the position which was adopted by the VRS from the JNA rules, from the very outset, from the moment the VRS was first established?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I've seen this document and a number of other documents coming from the -- from the -- from the corps that articulate similar -- this or similar type of activity. The issue is whether I saw any rigorous, robust and effective measures taken by the corps in order to implement this, and whether I saw investigations or prosecutions on incidents and events, some of which were directly referenced in the Krajina Corps documents and whether I saw any of this actually being implemented, and I didn't. I saw one or two small examples in the military prosecutor's court and the military court but those cases were -- were effectively dismissed or ---or were not fully investigated. And so I saw nothing that gave me the impression that these paper instructions were, in fact, followed and rigorously implemented. But I do accept, sir, your position, that this type of document -- there are a number of those documents which were written through the period that I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the archive. How much of the archive that belonged to the military prosecutor did you actually review?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I cannot remember in detail, sir. It was some time ago. I -- I certainly looked at the records in 1992, and I certainly looked at the records into 1993 for the 1st Krajina Corps. I can't remember how far on I went. It was -- it was actually some time -- time -- time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16585 receives number D435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D435 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document about this topic. Actually, two. The first one will be 65 ter 28410. The document was issued on the 21st of May, 1992. It comes from the 1st Krajina Corps Command. We need page 2 in B/C/S and page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's look at bullet point 10. I'm going to read in B/C/S -- it seems that the English version of the same text is somewhat shorter. I'm reading bullet point 10: "Provision of war-time units should follow the standard procedure. Looting or other criminal acts on the ground should be strictly prohibited." Would you agree with me that this part of this document says that the 1st Corps, in no way, wanted to resupply its coffers as a result of looting and robbery. It does not wish that to happen; i.e., this is contrary to your findings proffered under 2.186, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. So what happened in this section of the report is that I state that there were -- setting aside whether General Talic stopped the issue of looting in terms of investigating and prosecuting people, setting that aside, which is a different issue, what I argue is that General Talic issued instructions through his corps to prevent the issue of looting. And I argue that he was unhappy about individual looting occurring in his corps and issued these types of instructions. Now, why he did that, he's a military commander. Issue of looting is an issue of discipline as much as it is about criminality. So I argue that he issued these instructions but he was happy to follow the policy of the government, which I articulate in the section here, which was that movable and immovable property was to be taken and centralised and used for the benefit of the RS state. And that was a policy that he was happy to follow and requested his soldiers to follow. So he was unhappy with the issue of individual looting, and he passed out a number of instructions to that. Whether those instructions were effective, they were not. There was no prosecutions, no senior commanders convicted. Nothing. So I argue that he did pass these instructions out. But concurrently with this, what he did was asked his soldiers to follow the government policy which was to take movable and immovable property, to centralise it for the benefit of the state. And that movable/immovable property was incredibly wide-ranging. It wasn't just about abandoned apartments or military vehicles that could be commandeered, it was a wide-spread array of materials, including money, gold, and other personal items. So, on the one hand, I differentiate between this issue of him passing instructions relating to military discipline of his corps, and I differentiate that from what the RS government was doing which was taking large amounts of movable and immovable property through a formalised process which he was happy to support. That's the argument I put in that chapter, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe it's already Exhibit P2873.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no need to pursue that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more document op this topic. 65 ter 16574 from the Prosecution list. It's, again, a document of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the top, we see in the introduction: "From the Main Staff of the VRS of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "We have received a document stressing the need to vigorously oppose crime." And in the fifth paragraph, we read: "The Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is resolutely determined to eradicate such occurrences ..." The next paragraph: "Disciplinary action must be taken against every perpetrator of such offences, or in cases of serious offences, criminal proceedings must be instituted." Further down: "The organs of the military police and security organs are duty-bound to take measures to uncover these offences and their perpetrators, whereas confiscated stolen goods, objects, money and other items and the profit shall be confiscated against a receipt." We see that these orders constantly insist that this phenomenon must be eradicated. We have seen many documents that were not meant for the public eye that were documents for internal use repeating the same thing. According to you, these orders keep being issued while the same commands that issue them keep approving theft and keep tolerating it. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this document talks about the issue of all looting, including looting of Serbian army -- other properties, weapons, ammunition and equipment. So, again, I go back to this issue that individuals making profit, war profiteers, individuals operating on their own, I argue was not something that the Main Staff or the 1st Krajina Corps were -- were comfortable with. But come the middle of July when the Bosnian Serb authorities passed their instructions saying that all movable and immovable property, including money and gold and all sorts of other issues, are to be centralised and used for the state and that they pass that down to their soldiers, that's what I argue. I don't -- I don't doubt these documents that -- but what they don't want to do is -- individual speculators making money out -- or taking advantage of the opportunities. But when it comes to a state process by which similar types of property are centralised and used for the state, they're happy to go along with that. That's my argument. Looting is, in part, a military discipline issue, so it wouldn't surprise me that in a way the Main Staff and the 1st Krajina Corps are putting these instructions out because it does cut to the issue of military discipline as much as it does to the issue of criminality. But I go back to my point that these instructions, even setting aside whether these instructions had any effect at all, and I didn't really see that they did, I differentiate between individuals and their dislike of individuals making -- taking the opportunity to enrich themselves from that of the Bosnian state's position where, in the middle of June, they pass instructions saying this stuff is to be centralised and used for the benefit of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, there also comes point if you keep putting these instructions out and nothing happens, these instructions become meaningless. If soldiers know that -- that, yes, there's -- these instructions could come out but no one is really charged, and, importantly, no senior people are charged, these are -- or investigated and subsequently prosecuted, these instructions become meaningless. They become worthless. And there were a number of these instructions which I did not see being followed up by robust investigations, and not just investigations in relation to the low-level perpetrators, but significant -- significant investigations that result in senior officers being held accountable. Not because they themselves may specifically have been involved in looting but they are responsible for the activities of their troops. I saw none of that. And so if these instructions and similar ones to it are pushed out week after week after week with nothing happening, that there's not been a diminishing -- diminishing in terms of the criminality, and that there is no apparent robust and serious investigations, in particular against senior officers, then what happens is these instructions become pointless and meaningless and subordinates begin to know it. And so there are many areas about this issue of looting that -- that -- that this document talks to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it turned out that proceedings were instituted, then these instructions would not be meaningless, would they?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that they had to continually push out these instructions and that there were examples of looting that continued well into 1992, as I remember, and that I did not see senior members of the 1st Krajina Corps being held accountable for actions of their troops, I would argue that -- that they -- that they were not effective. A similar -- a -- a similar feature would seem to be also the treatment of detainees. There were examples in the Krajina Corps documents, including examples coming from the Main Staff, that the Geneva Conventions were to be applied, but despite those instructions, it is evident in their own documents that violations continued; and not only that violations continued, that I did not see any meaningful investigation or prosecution on -- on individuals within the 1st Krajina Corps, in particular, any senior officers. And -- and a similar -- a similar --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're explaining the same thing for the fourth time now. Have you seen any proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't ask that. The question was if it turned out that proceedings were instituted, then these instructions would be -- not be meaningless, would they. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the witness has explained to us that -- it's a hypothetical question. If there are any meaningful proceedings against those persons, put them to the witness and ask him whether that changes his mind. Because he did not say that never, ever, any action was taken at whatever level. But if you have a body of arrests, a body of -- a number of cases that were prosecuted in 1992, direct action taken against those who were suspected of having committed looting, then put that to the witness instead of if proceedings were instituted. I mean, it is hypothetical. If there are examples, put it to the witness. And not one very low-level case because he admitted already that some cases were then dismissed and exceptionally something happened but not meaningful. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] I would now like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16574 receives number D436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D436 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, if you ask these questions to the witness, then it's only fair to the witness that you put to him what your case is. Is your case that the witness is wrong because there were serious investigations, there were serious prosecutions, people were arrested, et cetera, you should put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have time to go into details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- it's not a matter of details --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll have our case. I have time for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, you do not understand that if you examine --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Whenever I give [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please don't interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I said don't interrupt me. Let's start with that. Mr. Lukic, under the Rules, if you are seeking evidence, testimony, in support of your own case, and if the witness contradicts that case, the Rules require that you put to him what your case is in this respect. So, you have spent a lot of time on totally irrelevant issues. You have ignored, more or less, what the real -- real concerns are, and the real issues are. Put to the witness if it the Defence case that serious investigations, arrests and proceedings were undertaken. Put it to him, then he can respond to it. And if you have concrete examples of it, put it to him as well so that we don't lose ourselves in hypothetical areas. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think I put our case in front of this witness, and we have our case to prove it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he still stands that he never saw any investigations, how can I change that. That he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what he said. That's not what he said. He said, At that time, I saw, apart from a few examples, I did not see for any higher-up level military persons to be investigated, to be arrested, to be prosecuted. And if you have such cases, you should put it to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask you something about your paragraph 1.131, where you talk about the removal of the leaders of the Muslims and Croats' community who had to be sent to vacation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know where should I repeat from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Repeat the whole question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Point 1.131. You talk about the removal of non-Serbs from the Army of Republika Srpska. You were asked about this in the Brdjanin case; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it was a few years ago, sir, but I do think it was a topic that came up. I can't quite remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Ackerman, suggested to you that it's normal to require army members to be loyal to the state, that they had proven themselves in combat, and that they have the citizenship of Republika Srpska. And you accepted that it's normal to require that from men who were to stay on in the Army of Republika Srpska. Would you accept the same today? If you want me to, I can show you the transcript of that session.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem. I'll -- I'll accept that was the -- the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, it was suggested to you, and numbers were cited, that 37 Montenegrins, 204 Yugoslavs, 62 Croats, 26 Macedonians, 33 Muslims, 13 Slovenes, 3 Albanians and 3 Bulgarian, 2 Czechs, 4 Hungarians, 1 Turk, 1 Jew, 1 pole, 1 gypsy, 1 Ukrainian, and 21 undeclared by nationality, by ethnicity, stayed on in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that comes from the combat analysis readiness report. The numbers seem incredibly small in relation to the overall strength of the army which was, I believe, in the combat analysis readiness report in 1993 was, I believe, about 180.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was also suggested to you that the criterion was not whether one was a Serb or not. Loyalty was the criterion. Would you accept that today, that loyalty was the criterion, not nationality?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military undoubtedly would expect loyalty as part of -- as part of their -- being a member of the military. But I think what I argued, I hope I argued at the time and I believe I argue in the report, is that, firstly, certainly in the Krajina area, there was a putsch from the ARK Crisis Staff to have non-Serbs removed from senior positions in business and other aspects in the Krajina and that -- that this emphasis had been placed on the VRS through Crisis Staff meetings and that that issue was sent up to the Main Staff for resolution. But what should we do about military individuals in the 1st Krajina Corps? And the Main Staff, on the basis of that request from the 1st Krajina Corps, passed down instructions that non-Serbs should go on leave back to Belgrade and that whether status would be resolved then, in reality, many -- I'm not saying all non-Serbs in the 1st Krajina Corps, certainly senior positions, were removed or left from -- from the corps. I think there were one or two who stayed on for a little bit longer, but certainly by late summer there weren't any non-Serbs in the 1st Krajina Corps in staff and senior positions. I think that was the argument I have in the report. But, you know, I do accept that loyalty is a component of -- of someone in a military. But you can be loyal and not necessarily be -- loyalty can -- we have, for example, Muslim soldiers in the British Army currently serving in Afghanistan. Maybe that, for some of them, you know, throws up questions of faith and other issues but they willingly do their job. Just because someone happens to be of a different faith or a different religion doesn't in itself mean that loyalty is questioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we're close to the point where we should take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Then we'll take the break now. Can the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Although it's not on the list of our documentation envisaged for this witness, with the Trial Chamber's leave, since you inquired about that. I would like to call up in e-court 10524. Before us is the report on the work of military prosecutor's offices for 1992. The report also contains a summary. The 1st Corps is on page 9 -- it begins on page 9 of the B/C/S and page 12 of the English. We need to go three pages further because it must be different in e-court. That is it. We have the right page in English. We see it says in the report the Military Prosecutor's office attached to the command of the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps. It's the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The document says, I quote: "In the said period, this prosecutor's office has submitted 559 requests to carry out investigations into 484 soldiers, 8 non-commissioned officers, 19 officers, and 48 civilians." It concerns a variety of offences. And we now need to move two pages on. We need page 11 of the document in B/C/S. And page 15 in English. Page 15 in e-court, in English. We see this is about crimes against property. The first paragraph says: "For this type of crime, 130 requests to carry out an investigation were submitted against 124 soldiers, 5 officers, and 1 civilian ... 18 indictments were issued against 18 soldiers. For this crime, no first-instance court ruling has been made."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know about these statistics of the prosecutors for the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you care for some advice from the Bench, are you wasting your precious time putting questions to this witness about this kind of report because you don't -- we don't know what the crimes are. Are these war crimes or just ordinary crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see -- what kind of property? Theft of a motor vehicle somewhere or theft of some ten loafs of bread somewhere. We don't know what kind of property this is. What the -- what the Presiding Judge asked you to do was to confront the witness with the record of cases where officers were prosecuted for committing the crimes that you have been saying they were warned against. Not -- not a report of the prosecutor but a record of the case. That's what the Presiding Judge asked you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will definitely do that during our case, Your Honour. I was just trying to see with this witness whether he has any knowledge about any of these cases. We can go to next page. There are concrete cases, but only five of them, I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the reason perhaps why Judge Moloto is asking, there are a few examples given. Half of them have got nothing to do with the kind of things Mr. Brown reported about, such as the theft of a truck from a depot. That is, of course, not the type of crimes Mr. Brown reported about. Similarly one of the other examples is that the theft of -- of a pistol, although there was, I see, a few -- there are cases which do fall within the category, apparently, but only four examples are given. Or are there five? And what we do see is that some do, some do not, on a total of 18. That is apparently what you put to the witness at this moment. To say that you'll present all this during your Defence case, as I said before, could the witness -- Did you know this report; and have you formed any opinion about the property crime cases which are briefly described here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, sir, if this is a document that included in my report or if I was aware of it at the time or it has came later. But looking at this refreshes here, 18 individuals from two corps, by the way, this is the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps. The level of individual annotated here is very low level. The numbers seem to be incredibly small, bearing in mind the problem that seemed to be existed in the 1st Krajina Corps' zone in relation to looting. I think this reinforced my point that -- that -- that these instructions, at best, were not followed and certainly that no senior officers were held to account for the issue of -- significant issue of looting that was clear in the 1st Krajina Corps documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, if I do understand it well from these examples, that the 18 soldiers made up a more limited number of cases, because I see in the -- I see in examples that there are often more than one accused so -- which would bring the cases, number of cases, apart from the number of persons investigated, down to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But those were only indictments. Eighteen indictments. And that's separate from investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And apparently no judgements whatsoever. Do you know the follow-up of these cases so as to see whether this ever ended up in a -- in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment. Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we go to page 18 of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many reports were filed in war time against an unidentified perpetrator when it was not possible to identify the perpetrator due to the war chaos? Did you deal with this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And there were references in some of the documents that perpetrators were unidentified. I assume that part of the task of investigations is to try and find that. But, no, there were a number of references to unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said this document is from 1993, not the period for which you reviewed documentation. You will agree with me, won't you, that the proceedings and identification of perpetrators could have taken place in 1993, 1994, 1995, or after the war. And in that case, your report would not cover such findings; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at the front of this document but I believe this is presumably covering the period of 1992 up until the writing of this document, which I think as you said was --

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- 1993. So this would seem to be that period. Doesn't cover what happened after. There could have been work relating to investigations that were ongoing that were not annotated in this document. As to investigations after the war, well, that seems to be quite a long time to deal with issues of significant criminality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In fact, you have no knowledge about the method and the speed of the work of the justice system in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia, do you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The study of the justice system wasn't part of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, going back, because I looked at the document, the property crimes in one out of the five cases, it says something about an enemy soldier, not an enemy civilian but an enemy soldier. For the others, I do not find any reference to the ethnicity of the victims. Now, it seems that it -- could you tell us, and looking at the names of the described victims, they do not immediately strike me as Muslim names, or is there a possibility that the majority of these cases were dealing with property crimes committed against other Serbs, or is there any ... which, of course, would -- would mean something in the context of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For that we'll have to go to the court records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you find any name which strikes immediately as a, for example, Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All accused persons are Serbs here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about victims, Mr. Lukic, to the extent they are identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no -- I cannot see any names of the victims. They said by-passers or prisoners. I don't see the names of any -- any victim names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the second case, sir, has got a name in it. The victim is a military conscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, in order to draw any conclusions as whether these are investigative activities which can be related to what the witness has described, we need more information. And the witness would need more information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was not studying this document anyways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But since you were -- I take it you have considered the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, this document was provided by my colleague, Stojanovic, who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Either you have or you have not put the right questions to yourself before you put the questions to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I brought this document only because of you, Your Honour. My intention was not at all. But now I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There we go. The mike took a moment to work. We clearly have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10524 receives number D437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, would it be imprudent if I asked -- if I could have a copy of that for the break to read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. If whomever could provide it to the witness. We'll make it available, then. The usher will give it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to go to your next part in your report, Manjaca camp, that is. Due to the restrictions in time, I will skip the first part. I may come back to it, time permitting. I'll go to the second part straight away, which is the part where you deal with Manjaca camp. I'll follow the sequence of the paragraphs. I'm not going to read them. First of all, paragraph 2.10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Lukic, you said no victim was named in this document. I see the name of a certain Mr. Djuric in the second item. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second item, the witness draw my attention to. There was one in the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I missed that at this moment. And that's -- doesn't strike me as a Muslim or specifically --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a Serb name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a Serb name. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 2.10. Did you come across the order issued in June 1992 to set up Manjaca camp, or did you base your conclusions only on the writings of Osman Selak?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I used the reference of Selak's notebook, sir. I did not see the specific instruction in the Krajina Corps collection on the establishment of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 211 -- 2.11. In General Talic's order to establish the war -- the prisoners of war camp at Manjaca, did you come across a portion which indicates that the Geneva Conventions have been violated?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- as I say, I didn't see General Talic's order specifically establishing the camp. There's a reference in Selak's notebook that a camp is to be prepared on that day, and I -- I know clearly that the camp was established in -- in early June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, is there any dispute -- is it the position of the Prosecution that General Talic's order contains anything which would indicate that the Geneva Conventions have been violated?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think we have a position on that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now paragraph 2.12 where you mention prisoners' camps in Prijedor, more specifically at Manjaca. You said that there were also Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, were those centres established by civilian or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were established by an instruction from the Prijedor Crisis Staff, which -- which had police/military/civilian presence. Well, whether it was the crisis -- yes, it was the Crisis Staff. I believe those reception -- or those camps were established on that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is your testimony here today that any of the military personnel were members of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor? And I'm putting it to you, sir, that they were not.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crisis Staffs are not really the -- the subject, per se. The subject or detailed analysis of the Crisis Staffs are not, per se, the subject of this report. What I can say in Prijedor is that Colonel Arsic and Mr. Zeljaja were present in meetings. Whether they were national defence meetings, whether they were Municipal Board meetings, whether they were Crisis Staff meetings, they were involved in these meetings with SDS representatives and police representatives in Prijedor. And, in particular, Colonel Arsic had been involved in the take-over the Prijedor at the end of April. So I would not agree with you that they were -- these military personnel were not members of the Crisis Staff. Well, formally -- whether there was a formal process of appointment, I can't say. That's not really the expertise I have. But I do know that these military men in Prijedor, the commanders at least, were present in these decisions and I'd have to go back to this document about the establishment of camps, but I believe that there was military representation at that specific meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no document on establishment -- there's a document that was signed by Simo Drljaca on the 31st of five [as interpreted], where he cites a decision of the Crisis Staff, but let's not go there. Did you see a document clearly indicating who members of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor were? I'm putting it to you again, sir, loud and clear, that that list of the members of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor does not contain the name of any of the military personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question. He doesn't know the formal composition of the Crisis Staff, and he stressed that military were present during meetings. So he has answered that question. He ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Soldiers did not attend meetings of the Crisis Staff. Perhaps only two or three times did they attend throughout all that period. And this is what I'm putting to the witness as I ask him:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know how many times did any of the soldiers attend a meeting of the Crisis Staff? And please bear in mind that you are confusing the Council for National Security or Defence and the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number of times military representatives were present at Prijedor Crisis Staff meetings. I do know that military representatives were present at the National Security and Defence Council meetings. How many times that was, I don't know. I just refer back to my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Do you know that the National Security Council stopped operating when the Crisis Staff was established because the -- that body was a body of the municipality of the assembly of the municipality, and the Crisis Staff actually replaced the assembly of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whatever the body was called, whatever the iteration and the development of the various bodies in Prijedor, it strikes me that there was a body that involved SDS, local police, and, at times, military representatives in decision-making in Prijedor municipality, irrespective of what the name of the -- the function was. But in -- I just go back to my answer that this is not a report about the workings of Prijedor Crisis Staff, Prijedor national defence meetings or other bodies. There are other experts who I know were working in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now paragraph 2.13. Did you come across a document which says that the Main Staff of the VRS had something to do with the establishment of Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't have an instruction or have seen a military document in the Krajina collection from the Main Staff around that period, the 1st of June, indicating that the Main Staff had ordered its -- its establishment. Of course, the document on the 12th of June from the Main Staff establishing prisoners of war camps throughout the various corps was disseminated on that day, and I think I argue in the report or present in the report that General Talic passes that instruction on to Manjaca camp and to the assistant commander for morale within his corps. So the camp has already been established by the 12th of May. That document is important enough to be sent down to Manjaca camp indicating that it is clearly already in existence, but, in relation to the 1st of June or the very initial day of its establishment, I have not seen a Main Staff instruction requesting that that camp be -- that camp be established. It is of note, however, that the 1st of June Selak entry, which would appear to indicate that that was the day the camp was expected to be established, is the day before General Mladic visits Banja Luka, that is the 2nd of June, he visits Banja Luka and there's a reference in his own notebook that he is in Banja Luka with -- speaking to commanders and officers of the corps. So maybe it's the context there, but the specific question of have I seen a Main Staff instruction establishing Manjaca camp, no, sir, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a report coming to the Main Staff from any of the camps, including Manjaca, Keraterm, or Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean camp-level documents going direct to the Main Staff, sir, or do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have. I -- I -- I -- I don't believe the camp documents that I reviewed indicate that they went to the Main Staff. And, actually, I wouldn't expect that. There is a subordinated chain, which would run from the Main Staff, to the corps, to the camp. And the documents from Manjaca camp that I have seen indicate that they go from the camp, to the security department of the corps. So -- which would sit in that subordinated chain as I would seem to expect. But, no, the documents that I've seen specifically from the camp, I do not -- I cannot say whether they went to the Main Staff because they're not annotated in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Omarska and Keraterm camps were managed and guarded by the police?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe, and certainly in relation to Omarska, that the police were the -- the guard -- guarded the -- the camp. There were references or there's at least one reference that the military provided some assistance; for example, in the laying of mines and also, I believe, in relation to joint investigative bodies. But, in relation to the guarding of camp, certainly at Omarska, I -- I believe that that was run by the police. I am not quite so sure about the set-up in relation to Keraterm camp. I believe it was something of a joint camp, but the actual functions within it, I'm -- I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.21, you discuss an instruction which was sent by General Mladic on the 12th of July. Do you remember that that instruction also includes a -- an order to prevent any breaches or violations of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I -- I do remember that, and that is what it says. In fact there had been a previous instruction sent by the Main Staff on the 4th of June which specifically dealt with wider criminality. But within that Main Staff instruction on the 4th of June, there was a direct reference that they had received information about violations against civilians and prisoners of war and that -- amongst other things, and that the 1st Krajina Corps received that instruction and passed it down to units of the -- of the 1st Krajina Corps. So this 4th of June instruction which is referenced in my Krajina report on this 12th of May instruction does make reference that Geneva Conventions are to be abided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And -- and now about your paragraph 2.36, which is the operative handling of inmates. Do you know, or did you know that the reception of prisoners of war at Manjaca was dealt with by a commission; and do you know who the members of that commission were?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't specifically know who the members of that commission were. The Manjaca documents indicate that there was a processing team that reported on their work, usually daily, and I am assuming that that would involve the interviewing of detainees and reviewing if there were any files that had been sent. But, in terms of the exact individuals who were part of that process, I'm not clear on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now just briefly let's go to the part that you yourself marked as status. The paragraphs are 2.41 through 2.45. Is it true, sir, that the command of the camp warned everybody that people were being brought in without any prior selection or screening process, that a large number was brought in, and that a lot of the documents show that people brought to the camp and that their escorts were civilian police officers?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it is the camp commander, but whoever is writing the reports are warning in a number of those reports, sometimes in significant detail, that large numbers of individuals who are being brought in did not deserve to be there, were rounded up from their homes or fields, and in significant details that were not combatants, were not carrying weapons or in uniform, some who were minors. So there are significant a number of reference, I believe, in the documents that I reviewed from Manjaca camp indicating that the author of that the report - whoever that was - knew that and was passing that information to the 1st Krajina Corps. The second issue is: Was I aware that the documents show that the escorts were civilian police officers. The documents don't always say who's brought the individuals in. In some cases they are escorted by the police, most notably the incident on the 7th of August, when detainees from Omarska were brought and there were deaths during that -- that -- that transfer. There are, I believe, a number of other documents which indicate the engagement of the police, but it doesn't always say in the documents, when they've received individuals, who's brought them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now 2.46. Is it true that even before the 6th of August, before the media campaign that you cite, the camp command carried out a screening process and warned that people who were being brought from Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most fell into various categories?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- they themselves don't necessarily always clearly differentiate the categories, but the reports clearly indicate a large number of individuals who are not combatants. Who are, in effective, civilians who had been rounded up and sent to detentions. That's one large number. They do make occasionally references to individuals who have been interviewed who they -- they deem as having been part of an armed resistance or a paramilitary -- whatever they phrase it, I can't remember. I haven't looked at the documents in detail for -- all of them for -- for some time. But that is a category of individuals, relatively small in numbers. So in that request, generally, there is that differentiation but there isn't a -- the biggest bulk seems to be or the biggest problem they come across are people who are not prisoner of war, i.e., combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The focus of my question was that there were warnings about that even before the media campaign. And in your footnotes 159 and 162, you cite daily reports dated 8 and 9 July, in which the screening process problems are indicated. What I'm trying to do is to establish that that problem was highlighted by the camp command, even before any media campaign started.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now paragraphs 2.49 to 2.51. When it comes to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, they requested from the police structures to send their representatives to the camp and to carry out a selection among the individuals whom they themselves had brought to the camp in the first place; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular section within status is -- is highlighting that even though in -- in early -- in an earlier period, for example, the July period that you mentioned, that it was known by the Krajina Corps that a large number of individuals, in essence, didn't deserve to be there and were civilians who had simply been rounded up and sent to the camp, that this resolution of their status was still not -- had still not occurred by the middle of August. Now, later, this 20th of August period, later on, is referenced in more detail about why this meeting on the 20th -- 19th and 20th comes around. It strikes me from the chronology of the events that it wasn't because the Krajina Corps who had highlighted this problem som -- or at least had been made aware of this problem through the camp records some time ago, this wasn't somehow being resolved that it just happened to take that length of time to August to resolve it. The 20th and 19th meetings are about the -- the -- are related to the revelations that came in early August and the criticisms that became apparent and the pressure that was put on the Bosnian Serb authorities in relation to detainees. So I -- it's a complicated chain. I reference it in this section to show that the issue had not been resolved in the -- in the camp. But later on, I explain why 19 and 20, in particular, was -- why this selection process occurred, and I argue that the selection process occurred not because the corps was necessarily trying to resolve it based on its previous -- its previous reports that it had received but it is related, in time, to the allegations and the pressure that was mounting on the RS authorities as a result of activity that happened in early August. I apologise for that long explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is -- is the issue you're dealing with whether Manjaca was a military-run camp or a non-military-run camp? Is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not. Then what exactly is the issue? Because then it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe in my next question [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you put clear questions so that we know exactly what you seek to elicit as evidence from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you've heard what the Presiding Judge is interested in. My next question was to be, and will be, this request directed at the police that they carry out a selection, does it indicate the powers of the camp administration over all the detainees?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the -- the question, particularly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe it's unartfully posed. [Interpretation] Why doesn't the camp administration carry out this selection themselves? Why do they, instead, call on the chiefs of the secretariats of police to ask them to carry out the selection? Do you find -- is it clear to you where the line is between the jurisdiction of the camp administration and the powers of the police?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I -- I can't necessarily deal with the issue of jurisdiction. What -- what I can say is that the camp received an instruction via the 1st Krajina Corps from the Main Staff in order to review the detainees that were being held in Manjaca. And in order to do that, it requested police to come to the camp to have a conference or a meeting to review the files and status of those individuals. Now -- and those individuals came, and the meeting was held. What does that demonstrate to me? Well, that the camp is reacting to a Main Staff instruction through the 1st Krajina Corps. What does it tell me? That, in order to resolve this problem, or this issue, that -- and bearing in mind only 14 days, less than that, actually, 1400 prisoners had come from Omarska and had been held in that detention centre, which was guarded by the police and that the police had a role in that. That in order to resolve this, they wanted to get the files and individuals who had been involved with those prisoners in Omarska for a period of time to -- to -- to -- in order for them to carry out this task that had been set them. So they are requesting the police to come to jointly resolve or deal with the task that was set them, which is what they did. That's what the document tells me about this meeting. Does it tell me about the nuances of the relationship between -- the judicial relationship from the camps and who can task who? No. But it's clear that the camp in it -- in -- in reacting to its instruction from the Main Staff gets the police to do what it requires is needed to resolve the problem. And, again, I apologise for the long-winded response to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talk a lot, as if you were a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad I'm not a lawyer, sir. I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're now going to discuss the general conditions in the camp. General remarks; that's 2.72. In that paragraph, you say that it appears that, for two months, the detainees had a poor water supply. Is it the case that the corps made efforts to deal with the problem the water supply in -- in an area that was short on water?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry -- sorry. The reference to the section?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 2.72.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the corps was aware that the water -- the water supply was inadequate and, indeed, sent out two instructions in order to -- to try and resolve that. I forget the references here and the exact dates. This is in 2.69.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you: Do you know that the corps did a bacteriological analysis of the water?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And it did that on the 27th of July, or at least there was a document requesting that, I believe, on the -- on the 27th of July. And they requested, I believe, that a section of pipeline be -- be replaced or restored. I think 2 kilometres. And they -- they put in two requests, I believe, for this in late July. Now the timing, I think, is important because that comes after the 16th of July visit by the ICRC in which one of the issues they were critical of was inadequate water. Of course, it begs the question: Why do you set up a detention camp in the first place if the water supply is inadequate. But, yes, they did put out instructions about water, but I believe those instructions came after the ICRC visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the guards drank the same water, the soldiers who were there, and that it was brought in cisterns because it was in short supply?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- I'd have to go back to the two document, but I believe that in the report on the water system at the end of July, it makes mention that the water is inadequate and is having to be brought in by cistern. I can't tell you whether the guards drank the water from the camp in the cisterns or whether they were based at the barracks. There was a barracks in Manjaca training area, not that far from -- from the camp itself. I don't know what the water supply to the barracks was. Manjaca had been a farm. It was -- it was a -- it had been a JNA farm for the storage of cattle. I -- maybe that's one of the reasons why the water was not -- was not adequate there. But I can't tell you what the guards drank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now paragraph 2, item 77. If, when people were brought from Omarska, let's say to Manjaca, there were some dead, and they were brought by the police, that cannot be blamed either on the camp or on the 1st Krajina Corps. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it's not as easy as that, I think, sir. The specifics of the incident from the documents of the camp are that these individuals were brought to the camp. They arrived early. They were brought by the police, I -- I -- I -- I agree. They -- they arrived early. They were forced to stay overnight, and that overnight, killings took place on those detainees which was known by the camp authorities and was known by the camp commander and was reported to the 1st Krajina Corps, including some names of potential -- or at least, I think, reference to the police -- the police commander. The camp refused to take the -- the -- the bodies in, and later took the remaining prisoners. It would appear to be that -- from -- at least from the documents, and I can only go on the incident based on the documents I've seen, that the police escorts were the ones who committed the crime. But there didn't seem to be any attempt by the camp to immediately hold the perpetrators, to immediately secure the scene as some kind of crime scene, to immediately inform, say, the military police, maybe -- you know, the killings itself outside the camp was on a training area, a military facility, just because it's on the perimeter of the camp if it's on a military facility whether there's a jurisdictional issue here, a whole raft of the questions and issues that did not seem to be addressed. What happened from the documents were that the bodies were taken away the -- I think there's a reference in one of the documents that the bodies may have been dumped. The perpetrators would seem to be the police, from the documents. Clearly the police would have -- should have -- I -- I would have expected, have done some investigation. Did I think the military carried out appropriate and professional response? No. As I said, I don't think they called the military police, didn't keep the perpetrators where they were, didn't protect the crime scene --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I think, in short, your answer would have been the police committed the crimes. Whether the camp and the 1st Krajina Corps are without any blame, you doubt, because no adequate response was taken to what was reported.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's in four, five lines approximately what you told us in 30. Could you please try to be more focussed. And, Mr. Lukic, it certainly assists if you put focussed questions to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the military police has no jurisdiction to carry out investigations against civilians in structures like the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know the full regulations of the military police, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's legitimate answer. [Interpretation] Now concerning paragraph 2.79, when you talk about the use of detainees to do work and even construct fire positions around the camp, would you agree that the POW camp Manjaca was never in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, I would agree with you, sir, yes. There was no fighting in and around Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also in paragraphs 2.80 and 2.81, you talk about the use of detainees in the 1st Engineering Regiment to clean the power plant. Would you agree that in this case, they did not run any risk to their lives and they were not in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I would disagree with you. Jajce had had significant combat operation -- combat operations in and around that zone at the time, and in fact the hydroelectric dam, I believe, was -- was a key feature in a key area in which combat was occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll check that. The detainees, the prisoners, volunteered to go to work. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents don't -- don't make mention that the prisoners volunteered to do that, as far as I'm aware. And I would imagine that irrespective of whether prisoners volunteer for military work that -- that -- that type of activity should not be encouraged or supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should now like to move on to -- I began with paragraph 2.82. I'll now move to 2.85. That's the treatment of minors and elderly detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we do that after the break, Mr. Lukic. Take a break of 20 minutes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
