utterances.text: Mr. Brown, may I ask you to try to give as short answers as possible so we can finish this examination today.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 2.82 to 2.85 of your paper. That's the treatment of detainees, minors, and elderly people. Is it true - and we can see that from your footnotes from 208 to 212 - that the command of the camp proposed several times that detainees who are not fit for military service and those who are infirm be released from the camp.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were one or two references that that should happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I see five here, but ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- you count quicker than I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now paragraph 2.87. [Interpretation] Would you agree with me that there is no responsibility on the part of the camp command, or the 1st Krajina Corps, for the fact that members of the police had brought minors from Prijedor to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think it's as easy as that. I -- my -- I mean, there's two issues: One is the capture of the individuals initially and who did that; the issue of transportation is a second issue. But once the individuals are in the camp, they are certainly the responsibility of the corps -- or the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the camp administration refuse to take in these prisoners? What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure the camp could refuse to take these individuals. The -- the camp, I believe, should abide by the Geneva Conventions. The camp clearly could have refused. They could have clearly said, These individuals are not combatants and don't deserve to be in my custody. Or if they did take them on, to treat them appropriately, and -- in terms of quickly releasing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in the process of admission it was not clear, it was not known, who was a combatant and who was not; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear that the camp, when they were writing their reports were unaware in some cases that large numbers were, but during the process of their -- their work became very quickly clear that many were not combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So is it true that when they realised that a person was not a combatant, the camp administration immediately reported that to their superiors? We have it in your footnote 216.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the work -- the writing, those who wrote those reports indicated to the 1st Krajina Corps that many individuals didn't deserve to be combatants and didn't deserve to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree that the camp command was not responsible and they reported to the superior command anything they observed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was not responsible for what, sir? Strikes me the camp was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry. Probably something was lost in the translation. [Interpretation] Is it true that the camp command reported everything they found to the superior commands and that it was not to blame for anything. It was not guilty. They didn't hide anything?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are three different questions but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my latest question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the camp command did not hide anything, they reported everything to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know what other reports were written. The reports say what they say. Whether that's everything, I don't know. They're not -- they're not extensive documents. They're a daily report of what they are doing. So, taken in that context, yes. The camp, in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- Mr. Lukic, did you intend to ask whether they were hiding their concern about the composition of the body of detainees? They apparently were not. If that was primarily your question. The composition of who -- who were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would be more artfully posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Did they hide, what kind of detainees they had and they had concerned about whether they were appropriately detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think these camps are very revelatory, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant reports, not camps, sir, in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now let me ask you about 5.29 [as interpreted], treatment of prisoner, ill-treatment. Would you agree with me that the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and the camp command had nothing to do with the ill-treatment of those prisoners who were incarcerated at Manjaca camp when they were outside of the camp, those ill-treatments that happened beyond the perimeter of the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry. I don't have an objection to the question. Just the reference 5.29. I'm not quite sure what that means and I don't see a corresponding paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said 2.89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2.89 under the heading: "Treatment of detainees, maltreatment." Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp commander and the camp authorities had responsibility for the detainees inside the camp. Whether they were civilians, non-combatants, or whether they were combatants, the camp commander had the responsibility for those detainees. The camp commander and the camp authorities had the responsible for the actions of the guards and soldiers within that camp, and so when -- when we talk about those inside the camp, the camp commander and authorities did have responsibility for both those issues. Both -- now, the camp commander reported to the Krajina Corps. So in that respect, the Krajina Corps had a responsibility to ensure the proper functioning of the camp. The soldiers within the camp were members of the 1st Krajina Corps and, of course, the 1st Krajina Corps is a member of the VRS, under the authority of the Main Staff and General Mladic. So that deals with the issue of the individuals within the camp. The obligations, I believe, to look after the detainees. Now in relation to your second point which is the ill-treatment of those outside --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's my only question about responsibility outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you said inside as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No -- okay. What about the responsibility for mistreatment outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp authorities are responsible for the camp, any actions inside. The Krajina Corps is responsible for the actions of its soldiers. If the Krajina Corps is involved in detaining individuals, taking individuals into custody, which they did as part of military operations, the Krajina Corps is responsible for the safe treatment of those detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question: Did you come across a document in which you saw that the military police or any other members of the army ever brought people to Manjaca to be incarcerated there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the police escorted, in specific details, two of the convoys that brought individuals into Manjaca, the convoy on the 7th of August, and the convoy from Sanski Most, which I believe was in July. Now, I know that there were other prisoners brought to Manjaca outside those two large -- or two -- two transfers which specifically made mention of police escorts. There was a large number of individuals from bought from -- this is from documentary reference, from Stara Gradiska prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. Did they refer to military police or to police alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they just refer -- I'd have to go back to the documents again, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because that would bring it outside the scope of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. This issue of Stara Gradiska, I just wanted to highlight, there is a reference of a movement of prisoners from Stara Gradiska prison to Manjaca, bringing -- I forget if it is 900 or 600. It does not specifically say that those prisoners were brought by military police, but Stara Gradiska was a prison that was also -- or a detention centre that was also run by the military. So outside those three specific documented reports, I did not see documents specifically identifying the military police as -- as -- as bringing individuals in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that Stara Gradiska was a prison, and, as such, it was under the authority of the civilian authorities, and the army did bring people in there and they were kept there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous answer reads otherwise, Mr. Lukic: "Stara Gradiska was the detention centre that was also run by the military." So, therefore, that question has been answered. If it's incorrect, please challenge the answer, but don't ask for the same again. Or imply in a -- in a question something which is different from what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, Stara Gradiska was the prison before the war, during the war, and after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ask the witness. You just told us that it was a military-run prison. On what basis did you establish that, because it's the position of the Defence that it was not a military prison. You can ask that question, no problem. But do not imply in the next question something which the different -- the witness had not said. Please proceed. Perhaps you have heard my answer -- my question, as a matter of fact, where I suggested to Mr. Lukic. If you could answer that question to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Staff Gradiska was a prison before the war. During the operations in Croatia, the 5th Corps took it over and used it as a facility to hold prisoners from Croatia. It was also used in the early part, I believe, in the early part -- this is from documentation, from the early part of the conflict in Bosnia by the 1st Krajina Corps to hold detainees and the 1st Krajina Corps military police units were involved in that process, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, if I could, whilst I was in the break -- whilst I was in the break, Your Honours, I quickly looked at this document about military prosecutions and there is one reference in there of an individual who is a military police officer who -- in Stara Gradiska who is being -- who was being investigated because he robbed a -- a detainee there. I don't know if that adds a little bit to the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 15 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your input.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I will retract that, sorry. It was Banja Luka prison. It wasn't Stara Gradiska. I do apologise, sir. But my position still is that it was a military facility run by the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I see in your report that the military police transported detainees from Manjaca to Stara Gradiska prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's the other direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the prisoners came from Stara Gradiska to Manjaca, sir. The report didn't say that the military police, per se, were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... in that transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I must not have looked carefully enough. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2.89. How many ill-treated individuals were seen by the ICRC team when they visited the camp on the 16th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of July Krajina Corps report to the Main Staff does not identify specific numbers of individuals who had been maltreated. The 16th of July instruction references general concerns, including the treatment of prisoners. The later ICRC -- more fuller ICRC report that gives a more -- more detail, I'd have to look at the documents but references large numbers, I think, or numbers. It doesn't, again, note specific instances or specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at 2.93. Do you know that the guards of Manjaca and prisoners were given the same food that was prepared in one and the same place using the same ingredients?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't sir. And that would seem somewhat irrelevant. The regulations indicate that certain standards are being maintained for prisoners. I don't know what the -- the guards at Manjaca prison were fed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that there were shortages of all of bare necessities in Krajina before the corridor was opened; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you're -- if the nature of the question is that because of shortages that's why prisoners were not fed, I don't -- I don't subscribe to that, and neither do I from reading of Geneva Conventions subscribe that that is a reason not to feed prisoners. If you cannot hold prisoners according to the standard, you shouldn't hold them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that this was a dietitian or a specialist who checked the -- the calorie value of the food that the prisoner -- prisoners were given at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know there was dietitian. But based on the ICRC report, if there was one, he clearly wasn't doing his job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that members of the ICRC demanded [Realtime transcript read in error "remanded"] that even those people who had been convicted of the crimes that they had committed also be released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that is exactly the case. There is a reference in the 16th of July, that they -- they want to -- I forget if it was release or speak to individuals who they claim were individuals who had committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we may just correct the record, Mr. Lukic. At page 57, line 14, the word "demanded" is written as "remanded." I thought I heard the witness say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Demanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I heard you, Mr. Lukic, saying "demanded."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Demanded, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there any source for us to consult on that issue you just raised a second ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, the release of those convicted. And may I take it that you'd refer to those convicted and not having yet served any sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness was protected so [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me a page number then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have the page number. I will -- 051, RM051.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know -- or, rather, in its report, did the ICRC committee state that the representatives of Merhamet which was a Muslim charity organisation visited the camp several times every week?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the ICRC report didn't make mention of that. I do know and I think I report that Merhamet did visit. I don't think the documents make reference that they report -- that they visited every week but that they -- they did appear there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.103, you say that Ratko Mladic personally inspected the units of the 1st Krajina Corps; to be more specific, the command of the 1st Doboj OG. How far was that command from Manjaca at that moment; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in terms of kilometres. It is a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are also talking about the corridor, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about his visit there. Wasn't the only visit he had to the corps, I hasten to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, if we're speaking about this, the distance would be at least 200 kilometres, and the reason for his visit was the corridor. However, let's move on. Representatives of the ICRC insisted on the camp being closed down. They didn't have any suggestions as to where it could be moved. They didn't even know whether there were any such locations that the military could use to open replacement camps, if Manjaca, indeed, was to be closed.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure that's necessarily the -- the role of the ICRC. The ICRC are there to monitor the standards of detention centres and make recommendations where necessary. It is the obligation of the detaining party, in this case the VRS, to provide suitable accommodation to hold those individuals. Or if there's not suitable accommodation to ensure that they're released and transferred or -- or dealt with. It's not the ICRC's job to find suitable -- or to ask about suitable accommodation. It's for the detaining party --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay. [Interpretation] Talking about paragraphs 2.102 to 2.106. Let me ask you, did the command of the Krajina Corps take into account of what the ICRC observed and said about Manjaca? Did they invest effort thereafter to improve the conditions of life of those who were held at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe he did, sir, at least not initially. The key recommendation of the ICRC, of course, was that the camp was closed and that didn't happen until another six or seven months. There were some references in August, middle of August, we've talked about, where there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have that in your report, sir. Do you know that an infirmary was set up within the perimeter of the camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- it may be the RS's own investigation report makes mention of a small infirmary that was being used, but I believe that the ICRC report certainly identifies that medical facilities there are not adequate. And after the ICRC's report, I did not see in the documentation a significant change or building or moving of -- of any medical facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that over 8.000 medical exams were undertaken in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that from the documents, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was another medical facility, a triage or reception, outpatients' clinic, outside of the camp? Did you incorporate that into your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in which location was that, sir? Where? Outside the perimeter or the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Outside of the camp but not far from it. If that rings any bell, fine. If not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't hear about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Enes Sabanovic was a doctor, a Muslim. Do you know that he practiced in the camp as a medical practitioner?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the name but I -- I do remember one of the investigative documents -- or the ICRC documents makes mention of a doctor or some medical staff from the detainees being used for or operating for medical purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the clinical hospital centre in Banja Luka was also at the disposal of the camp's inmates, if they needed help, and that the Serbian doctors from this medical centre visited the camp to administer aid to the inmates?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that -- that the hospital in Banja Luka, which was some distance away, was put at that disposal. But I go back to the comments of the ICRC that they have significant concerns about the medical condition of prisoners and the medical treatment that they could receive. So despite having that hospital some distance away would not seem to be, from the ICRC's perspective, that individuals were being treated or else they would not have been reporting their comments as they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue, I tried to search on -- in relation to the witness you mentioned on the word "convicted." I found only one and apparently irrelevant place where that word appeared. I would very much like to hear from you where we find the evidence which shows that convicted persons -- that the ICRC claimed that convicted persons should be released, convicted persons that were detained at Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They did not ask in that way. They asked for four prisoners to be released and all those four prisoners were actually already being convicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the way in which you presented it earlier, I think. But apart from that, I would nevertheless like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in some of the documents from this report. I found it, but I don't know it by heart now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness could assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I think it could be referring to the 16th of July instruction that the Krajina Corps sent to the Main Staff where they report that the ICRC asked to see some individuals and -- or -- or be released, but they put in parenthesis the most -- or that they are being convicted. I think it is possibly in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if the parties could assist me in finding that document under any 65 ter number because ERN numbers are very difficult for us to -- to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the 16th of July report being described is P230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P230. I'll have a look at it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that those who were wounded, sick, and infirm were released from the camp very quickly after the visit of the ICRC delegation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe that was the case. There are still references to sick, seriously sick individuals, going into the middle of -- of August and I believe also into September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the sick and the wounded were released from the camp after the -- the ICRC visit?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there were discussions in August and September about the release of sick and wounded. Whether that was them all, the documents don't necessarily make it clear. There was a release, I believe, in September. I'd have to check the document again. Part of the reasons for that release was articulated that they were drawing unwelcome attention so there was a release. It wasn't quick. And -- and I believe it was done because of the unwelcome publicity that had been generated around the ICRC and other visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to move to the part of your report entitled: "Treatment of prisoners, deaths." Here, you make mention of various incidents. However, let me ask you: Is it true that only two persons were actually killed in Manjaca camp; namely, Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware from the documents that those two individuals were highlighted as being beaten to death in the camp. There are a number of smaller -- small number of other references to deaths but they don't make it clear as to the background to those. But -- but those two individuals are specifically named as being killed inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were some deaths of natural causes within the camp, and you mention those in your paragraph 2.118; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This individual is reported as having died of natural causes. I don't make any judgement on whether that was true or not, but that's what the document report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as the two who were killed, Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender, it is it true that the perpetrators were identified? Do you know that those people were on trial as a result of which they were sentenced for the murder of those two people?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As -- as often with a question like this, I think it would be helpful if Mr. Lukic provided a year when the Defence is suggesting the trial happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Isn't it true that we went through this in quite some detail. So just -- you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just asking this witness if he is aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then, I take it, there is no problem in putting objective details to the witness right away. Would that be, Mr. Traldi? Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our case that the trial took place several years after the war. I don't know when exactly. But the whole procedure was based on the facts and evidence collected immediately after the incident. We saw medical documentation. In this case that was compiled immediately after the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put it to the witness, Mr. Lukic, with the details. Of course, if it is somewhat after the war it may be relevant to know whether it was 2000 or 2007 or -- but were you aware of prosecution of persons held accountable for the killings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. And if it was after the war it would seem to speak volumes. I did not see any investigation, certainly no prosecution based on the information that was coming from the camp at the time. And I did not see anybody held accountable during it. And if it was after the war it would certainly seem to -- to me, at least, to have some [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But have you no knowledge about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Lukic, I'd like now having been guided by you through the -- to the portion where you said: "Is it clear that members of the ICRC demanded that even those people who had been convicted of the crimes that they had committed also be released from the camp?" The 16th of July report gives no basis for such a statement. I hope it says that the ICRC had not been able to speak to four persons. They were then allowed to speak to those persons and they were informed that they had been convicted, I think by a military court. Now, another part of the report says that the ICRC, for the bad health condition, asked for the release of 19 persons which are then described as most serious extremists, not as the persons who had been convicted, and we find that somewhere else in the report. So the question includes a reflection -- an inaccurate reflection of the evidence unless you point me to any other point where it can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not right now, Your Honour, but I think it was discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put it to the witness, Mr. Lukic, you should have verified for yourself where to find it. Otherwise you should refrain from putting it to the witness. And if I can find out in two minutes the sources you said you relied upon, then you could have done the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If this was the only topic. I think that you are aware that I didn't sleep these days working on these materials [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so I don't want you to object that I didn't do this diligently enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's on the record. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 2.160. After the first visit of the ICRC on 16 July, were they prevented from entering the camp? Was their work hindered in any way?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, sir. They had a second visit a little bit later, and I believe there were follow-on visits in August or -- or September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.170. The measures that were ordered on 3rd of August, 1992, were they being implemented in Manjaca for quite a while?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suspect they hadn't been implemented, else the ICRC in their comments would have come up with a different conclusion. I think the request on the 3rd is to try and demonstrate to the visitors that the camps were well functioning when clearly the ICRC had reported that they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move to 2.179, reactions to the revelations of the conditions in Manjaca and the other camps in Krajina. You talk about exposure. However, we've established that the camp command reported to the corps command on a daily basis about everything that was going on, including negative things. Is it your position that something was being hidden so it needed to be exposed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, now carefully read the beginning of 2.179. It talks about "this exposure." This exposure, as in the first sentence, explained as activities and conditions inside Manjaca camp came to the wider international notice primarily through the media and ICRC reporting. Exposure is used in a very specific sense here. Therefore, it's of no use to ask whether this exposure took place internally first. You have asked that question already. That question was answered already, that they did not hide anything and that the reports were revelatory. So, therefore, let's try to focus on what really matters. Not repeat things. Not misread parts of the evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2.183, you deal with the London Conference and its impact on the exposure of the camps in BH, the camps controlled by the Serbs. Is it true that, at the same time, Croatian and Muslim authorities were not allowing access to the camps that they controlled; do you know?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say from the documents that I know that that was the case. However, there is one reference in a Krajina Corps document, I believe, which is the 10th of August, which was sent to the Main Staff, which is from the morale officer of the corps. And it explains the situation in the corps in the preceding months. And within the -- within a component of that report dealing with camps, it makes mention of the problem of retaliatory action and the treatment of prisoners by soldiers because of two things -- well, a number of things. Because of the reaction of the international community and media in misrepresenting the conditions in camps, and because of the international -- or the Croats' and Bosnian Muslims' unwillingness to allow access to camps inside their territory. So the report makes mention that this -- they believed that is happening. So -- that is one -- that is one area that I do know that there was that allegation. I don't know whether that, in reality, was true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how relevant it is, is another matter, Mr. Lukic. Because if the Croats or anyone else has misbehaved, that in itself does not excuse or justify, unless there's any specific reason why it would be different here. Please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something about paragraph 2.214. Did a single seriously ill prisoner die in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I do not know of seriously ill individuals dying or succumbing as a result of their illness. Obviously the two individuals who were beaten were -- may be a separate issue. But in relation to those sick, I did not see references in the documents to individuals who succumbed to those illnesses. I don't know what relevance that really has, particularly because seriously ill is seriously ill. It's not okay to have seriously ill in a camp and it to be okay but as long as they don't die. I don't see individuals, from the document, that did succumb, in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now paragraph 2.232. That is, the closing in 1992. Regarding this paragraph, let me ask you this: General Mladic was prepared to go forward with the -- an all-for-all exchange. Did you know why it did not take place?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, re-opening in 1993; point 2.243. Was Manjaca, in 1992, opened primarily for humanitarian reasons? Is it the case that armed elements of the Croatian community were brought there, those who had fled from Mount Vlasic from an attack of Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the activity of what resulted in these individuals fleeing, but these were -- I'd have to re-read the sections, but these were Croats --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me put it differently. Do you know that the stay of the military-able men at Manjaca was in agreement with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. All I can say is that the reference on the 8th of June indicates that 900 members of the HVO and civilians fit for combat had been transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what are your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I don't necessarily draw any conclusions as to -- as to anything more than the documents indicate, that the camp was reactivated for a brief period of time to house what they called civilians fit for combat, members of the HVO, that 900 were transferred there for a short space of time and that the same camp commander who been in charge in 1992 was appointed as the commander for -- actually, he had been promoted but he had been appointed to reactivate the camp, but it only was reactivated for a very short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not include in your report that it was an agreement between the Serb and the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I ask you one question in relation to the persons that, as you describe in paragraph 2.235, that were removed after having been selected. I see three categories: That is, Croat prisoners of war; extremist Muslim prisoners of war; and then the third category is the Muslim prisoners of war. Now, earlier, in the report, you described that many people could not be seriously considered as prisoners of war because they have just been rounded up. Do you know where the civilian portion of the detainees is to be found? Or were they just all re-named prisoners of war for purposes of exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe -- I might have to go over this document a little bit again. But I believe what happened is the Main Staff put an instruction to have these categories remain. So this is the Croat prisoner extremists. But the remaining prisoners were to be taken away and -- these are the ones who left in the coaches and went over to Croatia. I think this is referring to an instruction to say, There should still be some individuals from the group in Manjaca that we need to keep, and that is these ones here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, that's 532 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the 532. And the remaining 1800, or whatever it was, were the ones that were transferred into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because I saw earlier in your report discussion was about an exchange with the exclusion of prisoners for whom it had been established that they had committed criminal acts. But a category of prisoners of war does not include that it would have been established that they had committed crimes, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's some inconsistency in the approach there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for the break. We'll take a break of 20 minutes and then we'll have another 55 minutes to go after that. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To focus re-direct planning, if I could just inquire if Mr. Lukic is on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we spoke that I will use 15 minutes during the next session and then I will give --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need, Mr. Traldi, for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have been making an effort to cut as we went, Your Honour. I think I'm at about a half an hour right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps if Mr. Lukic could even take slightly more time, that would not bring us into problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It might, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, I'd like to briefly deal with the Prosecution 11th motion to amend the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. On the 7th of November, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to seek addition for each document subject to the 11th motion to amend the Rule 65 ter exhibit list in court at a time when it wishes to use that document with the witness, Ewa Tabeau. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution did not seek the addition of any documents with Witness Tabeau, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Prosecution to the extent that it intends to tender some of these documents, to request their addition to the exhibit list in connection with the request for their admission into evidence. To the extent that the Prosecution has already requested their admission in a pending motion, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to specify which document and motions are concerned. And, under these circumstances, the Chamber denies the Prosecution's 11th motion to amend the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, without prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. Brown, that we dealt with other matters when you are coming in. Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not trouble you much longer. Let me ask you, first, looking at the transcripts of your earlier evidence and the description of your job, I concluded that your job in the Prosecution was both investigative and analytical. Is it true that you interviewed witnesses?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in a number of interviews as a support to investigators and Senior Trial Attorneys, or lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you also interviewed witnesses in the cases where you acted at the same time as an expert?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was part of an interview team, yes, I was, sir, of a number of -- a small number, actually, of military witnesses that the Office of the Prosecutor felt, due to the work I was doing with documentations and my previous military service, that I might be of use to them, so I took part in a number of interviews with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, the simple answer being yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding the drafting of your reports, I will put to you what I have found, and you will tell me if that's correct. You would first write up a report, then you would have meetings with the OTP where you discussed with the members of the Prosecution the content of the report, and, during these meetings, your report would be finalised. After that, it would be disclosed to the Defence. Was that the procedure or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes. To all intents and purposes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of preparing these reports, you made two erratas. Do you have your errata reports on you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have these errata reports with me, if I want to have them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, sir, I don't think I have mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here you go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, on the screen, if possible, we should pull up P2859, your report. We need paragraph 1, item 1.17. It's your first report on the Bosnian Krajina. Page 16 in English. Page 17 in B/C/S. A document is linked to this paragraph, and it's in footnote 17. My colleague, Mr. Ackerman, at the Brdjanin trial suggested to you that it was the wrong document; that is to say, this footnote is not correct. Would you agree that this part of your report should be corrected too? And the referenced document does not relate to what it purports to relate to in paragraph 1.17?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be the case. Maybe I haven't completed the errata. I'd have to go back to the document and look at it. Maybe that is an omission on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, footnote 17 has been corrected. You are aware of that? Errata sheet, first page, bottom, footnote 17 should read ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear you, Mr. ... it has been corrected, although without ERN numbers, apparently. But it's now the 5th Corps' regular combat report. What else would you like to have been corrected, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was checking those documents, when I was checking everything, and I didn't find ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We didn't hear what you didn't find, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have a correction. If there's anything to be added to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Right now, I cannot ... cannot check it. Paragraph 1.112.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say in this paragraph that communications, like at the municipal level, were established in a similar way between regional organs, including the organs of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And you mention the 14th of April, 1992. My colleague, Mr. Ackerman, suggested to you that, at that moment, the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina did not yet exist. Would you agree that this is an error in your report, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see 1D1469 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would assist you. That is your testimony from Brdjanin case; 27th October, 2003.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know exactly when the Crisis Staff was established, if there's a slight error here. My point is more that the ARK -- the corps has a relationship there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably you -- you knew better at that time, ten years ago, because you were specific. Can we -- yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need page 64 in e-court and it's page 21542 from the Brdjanin trial. We need lines 2 to 5. We have to go one page ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question was: "We are going there, but I'm talking about 1.112 right now. We are talking about April of 1992. There wasn't even an ARK Crisis Staff at that point, was there? "A. No, I don't believe there was." [Interpretation] Does that refresh your memory that at that time the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina did not exist and, consequently, this paragraph is erroneous.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it might be erroneous in terms of the Crisis Staff, but that is not the emphasis of the report or that section. But, yes, I accept that. I'm more than happy to amend that report and put Autonomous Region authorities instead of Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1.113 deals with the visit by Tadeusz Mazowiecki. Do you recall now whether that visit took place on the 23rd of August?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was an attempt by him to visit, which was denied to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, consequently, the members of the Crisis Staff of the ARK could not be present either.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe he accompanied Mr. Mazowiecki in his attempt to visit the camp, from what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you believe nothing should be corrected here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I think this paragraph is being slightly mischaracterised. The same information the witness just provided is in the footnote to the paragraph 187 which recognises that the visit was denied and says the report that's been cited notes that one of the Crisis Staff members was involved in the organisation of the visit. So I think the report and Mr. Lukic are in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I know, that -- and what was suggested that what is mentioned here in the report is not correct, that the members of Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff actually visited Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look. Paragraph 187, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Footnote 187 is the one that I[Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 187. Yes, that's what I thought I heard. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Lukic is now referring to footnote 186. You're contesting that the -- Predrag Radic -- that the president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina visited the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's at 186. And -- and the -- the witness refers there to the 1st Krajina Corps regular combat report dated the 9th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, in this report, should it be that they visited lower Manjaca or not? That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- it seems that -- It seems that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... could we just try to cut this short. It seems that in the footnote, perhaps as a correction, you have now reported that the visit was denied, whereas, in the main text, the visit still is presented as having taken place. Is that an error?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that could be an error, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.18. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was suggested to you there that disarmament was supposed to take place only in non-Serb areas, and you cite a document in footnote 272. At the trial on 28 October 2003, transcript page 21610, lines 15 through 17, you accepted that the document doesn't show that this order to disarm applies only to non-Serb regions. Footnote 273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, of course I cannot follow what -- the testimony in another case. I notice, on the basis of your question, that the text now reads, "Also," which seems not to be a reference to exclusively disarming of, as you said, non-Serb areas but that the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But army also should take part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- also has -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... also non-Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, depends then on how you read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You could also read: The army also had a role to play in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's -- Any comment from the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was using the document, the reference -- I can't remember the exact document itself, but I think it makes mention that the military are to be involved in the disarming process. I'm using the footnote to demonstrate that the army are to be involved in that process. I'm not using the footnote to demonstrate that it's non-Serb areas attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's see 1D1470. It's the transcript from Tuesday, 28th October 2003, Brdjanin trial. We need page 50 -- 45 in the e-court, lines 14 to 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that you accepted here that you made mistake.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- as I say, I think I was using the footnote to demonstrate a different issue within the text. But without seeing the document again, I will take at face value it doesn't say "attack non-Serb areas." But I think the reference, the emphasis of the sentence, is that it's this issue of police and military co-operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree that it would have been more accurate to correct a new version of the report so as to clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or to put the footnote through the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are there any more mistakes in your report? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my report, sir. I'm sure that there will be footnote references and smaller issues that undoubtedly will be in there, and I'm more than happy to make changes as necessary. But the underlying aspects, I would stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 1.31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'll not stop you at this moment, although you're already living in Mr. Traldi's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll do this one and then I'll stop. And so we need footnote 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd note that this one we put on the record at the beginning of direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah. One of the first questions I asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It was a long time ago. I forgot. Then paragraph 2.5 and footnote 239 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you still had one in reserve, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have many. I have no time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why not sit with Mr. Traldi and assist together the Chamber in removing errors which are of greater or lesser importance? The Chamber is open for that. But you're asking for 2.5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And footnote 239.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And on the 14th of July, 2005, in Krajisnik trial, on transcript page number 16517 - if you want, we can see it - you admitted that that is wrong reference. We can see -- I'll finish here just to show you the transcript, 1D1471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a wrong reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a wrong reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then why not try to find the proper one or strike the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I exceeded my time. Mr. Brown, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much your patience, sir. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber also appreciated that at the very end you started even improving the quality of the work of the witness. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To focus re-direct I have proposed to Mr. Lukic that two documents be admitted from the bar table, 65 ter 16489 and 16582. I understand that the Defence would reserve the right to litigate the weight to be afforded these documents, but it would allow us to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you immediately that we have no objections to the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 16489. It's military document. But we have many issues with the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have issues or do you objections against admission, which is not the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Against -- we have objections against admission as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And them being what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because it's multiple document signed by different people. So it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see it here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see that you now know that there is some problem with the admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can't -- I have got no idea what it is at this moment, so you have to assess how to proceed, whether to keep on the same -- safe side and deal with it with the witness, or to take the risk that -- and tender it from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's a compilation of several official records, so I may take the risk, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But I -- I would ask that 16489 be admitted at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar. The number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2888, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then, sir, I'd ask that we start where Mr. Lukic left off with one of the purported mistakes in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 06493.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While this comes up, I'd ask you, did you ever see an indication that any disarmament operations in late May were conducted in Serb areas?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this document, now that it's up, starting in paragraph 1, notes that various Bosnian Muslim forces have been: "Disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations in the Sanski Most municipal area." It describes that in the next paragraph and then says: "On 25 May 1992, this 'disarming' was followed by a military action (attack) against the down-town neighbourhood of Mahala ..." Based on your knowledge, is that a Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "Which resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians, but no significant amount [sic] of weapons have been found because they had been concealed earlier." Is this document consistent with your conclusion that these disarmament operations were targeted at non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered 65 ter 06493.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2889, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30215. It is an article by Roy Gutman dated 19 July 1992 titled: "There is no food, there is no air."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up, sir, Mr. Lukic suggested to you that no articles had been published about the detention facilities before 23 July 1992. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And does this document perhaps clarify for you whether articles had been published before that date?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem that Gutman, who was aware of Manjaca, was publishing an article at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tendered 65 ter 30215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2890, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2890 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30214, please. It is article also by Roy Gutman dated 19 July titled: "Prisoners of Serbia's war."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And does this document also clarify that matter for you, sir?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll tendered that document as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only I should maybe raise -- rise before, but I don't know what's the position? Can we introduce newspaper articles without questioning writers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the purpose of what Mr. Traldi is doing is to challenge the suggestion that the world would not have known yet and therefore the measures taken could not be in response to. That is -- seems the major purpose of this effort, Mr. Traldi, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the articles reflect that as of the 19th, if not earlier, conditions in the camp were known and publicised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you introduced the matter that the measures could not have been taken in response to, at least that was a suggestion in your questions, and that is what Mr. Traldi is now responding to. And not necessarily for the truth of the content of exactly what was published, is it Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be true. You may even think it's true, but that's not purpose at this moment of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, if there's any objection please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only this one that I think it's not common to introduce the media --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30214 receives number P2891, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2891 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, sir, Mr. Lukic suggested to you that non-Serb forces were stronger than you credited them for. Is it right that your evaluations of those forces' strength were made on the basis of VRS and Bosnian Serb documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to look at one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 06966.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This relates to the follow-on operations in Prijedor in late July 1992 which you discuss in your Krajina report. The document notes in page 1 in point 1 in both languages that the enemy has: "Respected the cease-fire in the corps' entire zone of responsibility." And then describing Prijedor specifically in the next paragraph says: "Muslim fighters, singly or in small groups, occasionally appear around the Kozarac and Kozarusa villages, attempting to make a breach towards Prijedor or across mount Kozara towards the Sava river." Is that consistent with the other documentation you've reviewed about the strength of Muslim forces in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 06966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2892, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to show you two documents now about these operations and ask a simple question after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 16935.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a report from Prijedor SJB at the beginning of July 1992. If we could turn to the next page in B/C/S and at the bottom of the page here in English, is it right there we see a list of weapons that have been seized by the Prijedor SJB as of that date?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 10851, a similar report at the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we can't go through every category for time reasons, but based on your recollection of these documents, do they indicate large number of weapons were seized by the Prijedor SJB in July or are the numbers pretty similar?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're relatively small numbers, but it's also the type of weaponry there, hunting, carbines, old M-48s and old rifle. So it's the numbers that are small and also the type of weaponry that is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd tendered those two documents. 16935 first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2893, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And 10851, second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2894, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now I want to turn back to Sanski Most. Could we have P2409, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this morning Mr. Lukic suggested to you that persons who left Sanski Most did so voluntarily. Do you recall that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And here we see under "Conclusions," point 1: "Mirko Vrucinic, Nedeljko Rasula and Colonel Nedjo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca." And it lists three categories: First category, politicians; second category, nationalist extremists; third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. Is there any reference here to international law or the principle that these unwelcome people shouldn't leave the municipality unless they choose to do so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it says they're being sent to Manjaca. Is this consistent with documents you reviewed from Manjaca as to what type of persons were held there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it would seem reflective of the documents in Manjaca themselves when they arrived and when they were processed that they knew that large numbers who were in the camp were not combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender P2409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah, it's MFI'd. It's an associate exhibit pending a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it's now admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Before focussing on Manjaca, I'll ask you about a couple of other specific camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 7131. This is a document emanating from SJB Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic suggested to you today that the Prijedor camps were essentially civilian camps. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Here on this first page at point 1, we see a reference to a provisional collection centre that will be set up at the Omarska mines strip mine. And at -- at point 3, rather, we read: "A mixed group consisting of national, public and military security investigators shall be responsible for the work with and categorisation of detainees. They shall organise themselves respecting the parity principle." And it refers to Mirko Jesic, Ranko Mijic and Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic who shall be responsible for their work. Do you have a comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem that Omarska camp is going to have this joint military security input in relation to investigating these individuals. Colonel Majstorovic was an officer in the Prijedor military garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 07131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2895, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 16627. This is a document identified as from Prijedor Region Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this document is labelled "Official Note," refers to Zoran Zigic, and is a report of allegations against Zigic. On the third point it refers to him as a private and says he was taken into custody. We see it's sent by the Prijedor Region Command to the security organ of the 1st Krajina Corps. What importance do you attach to this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zigic was a soldier within the Prijedor Region Command, and he is clearly been working in Keraterm camp and he has committed an extortion here and it is been reported up the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have a look at the date and see whether the translation needs to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I note, Your Honour, that the translation is missing the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless the parties would agree that the 13th of June, 1992, is meant -- which seems to be consistent with the first line referring to the 10th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree. Then it can be admitted with the caveat that the year should be 1992. Please proceed. Mr. Registrar, please give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2896, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 16633, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is identified as from the Official Gazette and coming from Dr. Stakic. At point 1 we see that Major Kuruzovic, commander of the Prijedor Territorial Defence, is relieved of duties as of 29 May 1992 and placed under the command of the command of the region. Would that have placed him within the VRS chain of command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Regarding Trnopolje, I'd refer Your Honours to adjudicated fact 1063, and I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we decide on that, can the president of a Crisis Staff put Mr. Kuruzovic in a position in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe the background to this would be it's a time when the Territorial Defences were being integrated into the VRS as was expected at the 12th Assembly session, and it comes a few days after that. Kuruzovic had been the commander of the Prijedor Territorial Defence, so I suspect that what was happening here was that there were negotiations into how we can and effectively merge the TO into the VRS. And he is being appointed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And command of the region in these circumstances means what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prijedor region command, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2897, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in the interests of time, sir, I'm going to just focus on a very narrow issue related to Manjaca. Mr. Lukic asked you about how prisoners were brought to Manjaca. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to focus on the type of prisoners who were kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30216.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the second paragraph it says -- we see the date, 2 July, 1992. The second paragraph, it says: "Processing of individuals from Kljuc municipality is coming close to its end." Were there any large releases in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tendered this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2898, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 07153, please, page 4 in the English and 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We discussed -- Mr. Lukic asked you about as well, the selections of prisoners in late August 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. And this, I think, will also relate to a question that Mr. President asked you on Tuesday, when it comes up. In the final paragraph, it says: "On 20 August 1992, we received a task from Major Pero Stupar, which was the result of a telegram from the Main Staff of the Serbian army, and related to our activities and engagement to realise the tasks received. In accordance with this telegram, representatives of the Bosanska Dubica, Kljuc, Banja Luka, Prijedor, and Mrkonjic Grad CSBs came to Manjaca camp." And then it describes a little bit about a joint meeting. On Tuesday, His Honour Judge Orie asked you, based on another document, whether, in your view, the military had a role to play in dealing with the revelations about conditions at Manjaca camp and you said you believed it did. Does this document reinforce your conclusion in that regard?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 07153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2899, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
